II-36.summary: PPHN is a term baby whose pulmonary vascular resistance never falls, so blood shunts right-to-left at the duct and foramen ovale: think of it when cyanosis is out of proportion to the lungs, prove it with a pre/post-ductal gap and echo, and break the hypoxia-acidosis-vasoconstriction circle with gentle care, oxygen without hyperoxia and iNO.

questions.stem: In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, at which sites does the abnormal shunt occur and in which direction?
options: Left-to-right across the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale
Right-to-left across a ventricular septal defect only
Right-to-left across the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale
Left-to-right through intrapulmonary arteriovenous channels
questions.explain: Pulmonary vascular resistance stays above systemic, so deoxygenated blood crosses the fetal channels (PDA and PFO) from right to left. A left-to-right ductal shunt is the picture of a preterm PDA once PVR has fallen.
questions.note: Right-to-left shunt at the PDA and foramen ovale.

questions.stem: What is the commonest underlying cause of PPHN in a term neonate?
options: Meconium aspiration syndrome
Transient tachypnoea of the newborn
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
Maternal SSRI use in pregnancy
questions.explain: Meconium aspiration is the commonest trigger. CDH and maternal SSRIs/NSAIDs are recognised but less frequent causes; TTN rarely produces significant PPHN.
questions.note: Commonest: meconium aspiration; also sepsis, asphyxia, RDS.

questions.stem: A term baby with PPHN remains at saturations of 78% despite FiO2 being increased from 0.6 to 1.0. What is the main reason the extra oxygen barely helps?
options: Fetal haemoglobin cannot bind oxygen at high partial pressures
Surfactant is inactivated by high inspired oxygen concentrations
Hyperoxia causes reflex systemic vasodilatation and worsening hypotension
Shunted blood bypasses the alveoli and never meets the inspired oxygen
questions.explain: The hypoxaemia is due to right-to-left shunting, so raising FiO2 cannot oxygenate blood that skips the lungs. HbF actually has a high oxygen affinity; the other options are not the mechanism.
questions.note: Shunted blood bypasses alveoli → FiO₂ barely helps.

questions.stem: A 40-week baby born through meconium-stained liquor is deeply cyanosed at 6 hours with saturations swinging between 70% and 90% with handling; the chest X-ray shows only mild changes. Auscultation reveals a loud single second heart sound and a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Transposition of the great arteries
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency
Transient tachypnoea of the newborn
questions.explain: Term baby, cyanosis out of proportion to lung disease, labile saturations, loud single S2 and a tricuspid regurgitation murmur is the PPHN pattern. TGA also gives cyanosis with a single S2 but saturations are not labile with handling and there is a meconium trigger here; echo will separate them.
questions.note: Term baby, cyanosis out of proportion to lung disease, labile saturations.

questions.stem: A cyanosed term baby is suspected of having PPHN. Where should the pre-ductal saturation probe be placed, and what gap supports the diagnosis?
options: Left hand; post-ductal higher than pre-ductal by more than 3%
Right hand; pre-ductal higher than post-ductal by more than 3%
Right foot; pre-ductal higher than post-ductal by more than 10%
Left hand; pre-ductal higher than post-ductal by more than 3%
questions.explain: The right arm is supplied before the ductus, so right-hand saturation is pre-ductal; a pre- minus post-ductal gap >3% indicates ductal right-to-left shunting. The left arm may be post-ductal and the feet are always post-ductal.
questions.note: Pre-post-ductal gap (>3%); pre-ductal = right hand.

questions.stem: A term baby has severe hypoxaemia, no pre/post-ductal saturation gap and a clear chest X-ray apart from a small heart. Before starting inhaled nitric oxide, which investigation is mandatory?
options: Hyperoxia test in 100% oxygen for 10 minutes
Cranial ultrasound to exclude intraventricular haemorrhage
Blood culture and CRP to exclude early-onset sepsis
Echocardiography to exclude cyanotic congenital heart disease
questions.explain: Echo confirms the shunt and excludes structural disease such as obstructed TAPVD, where iNO can worsen pulmonary oedema. A hyperoxia test cannot reliably distinguish PPHN from cyanotic heart disease, since both fail to rise.
questions.note: Echocardiography confirms the shunt and excludes cyanotic heart disease (TAPVD).

questions.stem: A ventilated term baby with echo-confirmed PPHN has an oxygenation index of 28 despite optimal ventilation and surfactant. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
options: Inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm
Inhaled nitric oxide at 80 ppm
Intravenous sildenafil as a first-line bolus
Immediate referral for ECMO
questions.explain: iNO 20 ppm is indicated once the OI exceeds 20-25; it relaxes pulmonary vessels via cGMP. Higher doses add methaemoglobinaemia without benefit, and ECMO is reserved for cases refractory to iNO and haemodynamic support.
questions.note: Inhaled nitric oxide 20 ppm if OI >20-25 (relaxes vessels via cGMP).

questions.stem: A term baby with PPHN on iNO has a mean arterial pressure of 32 mmHg and worsening ductal shunting. Which approach best addresses the haemodynamic problem?
options: Increase FiO2 to target PaO2 above 15 kPa
Give a sodium bicarbonate infusion to a pH above 7.6
Support systemic pressure with milrinone, adrenaline or vasopressin
Hyperventilate to a PaCO2 of 3 kPa to induce pulmonary vasodilatation
questions.explain: Low systemic pressure lets PVR exceed SVR and drives right-to-left shunting, so BP support (milrinone, adrenaline, vasopressin) is key; ECMO if refractory. Hyperoxia should be avoided, and deliberate alkalosis/hyperventilation are outdated and harmful.
questions.note: Support BP (milrinone, adrenaline, vasopressin); ECMO if refractory.

cards.front: Outline the management of PPHN step by step.
cards.back: Minimal handling, sedation, normothermia • oxygen but avoid hyperoxia • surfactant (e.g. meconium) • iNO 20 ppm if OI >20-25 • BP support: milrinone, adrenaline, vasopressin • ECMO if refractory.

cards.front: How do you diagnose PPHN and what must you exclude?
cards.back: Pre/post-ductal saturation gap >3% (pre-ductal = right hand) • echo confirms right-to-left shunt at PDA/PFO and excludes cyanotic CHD, especially TAPVD.

cards.front: List causes of PPHN and explain the vicious circle.
cards.back: Meconium aspiration (commonest), sepsis, asphyxia, RDS, CDH, maternal SSRIs/NSAIDs • hypoxia + acidosis → pulmonary vasoconstriction → more shunt → more hypoxia.

II-37.summary: Sort perinatal infections by route (transplacental, intrapartum, postnatal) and you know the bugs, the timing and the prevention: HBV vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours, intrapartum penicillin for GBS, aciclovir for HSV, no breastfeeding in HIV.

questions.stem: Which of the following infections is typically acquired intrapartum rather than transplacentally?
options: Toxoplasma gondii
Parvovirus B19
Rubella virus
Group B streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae)
questions.explain: GBS colonises the maternal genital tract and is acquired during passage at birth. Toxoplasma, parvovirus and rubella cross the placenta.
questions.note: Intrapartum: GBS, E. coli, HSV, HBV, HIV, gonococcus, chlamydia.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old baby develops copious purulent discharge from both eyes with marked lid swelling. What is the most likely organism?
options: Chlamydia trachomatis
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Herpes simplex virus
Staphylococcus epidermidis
questions.explain: Gonococcal ophthalmia presents at 2-5 days and is hyperpurulent; chlamydial conjunctivitis appears later at 5-14 days. Chemical conjunctivitis from silver nitrate appears within the first day.
questions.note: Gonococcal conjunctivitis 2-5 days; chlamydial 5-14 days; silver nitrate: chemical conjunctivitis.

questions.stem: A 10-day-old baby, previously well, develops lethargy, focal seizures and a few clustered vesicles on the scalp; transaminases are raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Late-onset group B streptococcal meningitis
Congenital cytomegalovirus infection
Neonatal herpes simplex infection
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
questions.explain: Seizures, vesicles and hepatitis are the classic triad of neonatal HSV. GBS meningitis lacks vesicles; congenital CMV is present from birth with petechiae and calcification; SSSS gives superficial peeling, not CNS disease.
questions.note: Neonatal HSV: seizures, vesicles, hepatitis.

questions.stem: A baby is born to a mother who is HBsAg-positive. What is the correct management?
options: Hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours; breastfeeding allowed
Hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours; avoid breastfeeding
Hepatitis B vaccine alone at the 8-week immunisation visit
HBIG alone within 72 hours, vaccine after maternal viral load
questions.explain: Vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours (at latest 24 h) prevents most transmission, and breastfeeding is permitted. Delaying protection matters because infants infected at birth become carriers in up to 90%.
questions.note: HBV: vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours (at latest 24 h); breastfeeding allowed.

questions.stem: Why is preventing vertical hepatitis B transmission at birth such a high priority compared with adult infection?
options: Infected infants become chronic carriers in up to 90% of cases
Neonatal hepatitis B is usually fulminant within the first week
Infected infants usually develop cirrhosis before school age
Hepatitis B causes major structural malformations at birth
questions.explain: Neonatal immune tolerance means up to 90% of infected infants become chronic carriers, with later cirrhosis and HCC risk. Fulminant neonatal hepatitis is rare and HBV is not teratogenic.
questions.note: Parvovirus B19 → fetal anaemia and hydrops; HBV in infants → up to 90% carriers.

questions.stem: A woman has an acute febrile illness with a lacy rash at 20 weeks; two weeks later the fetal scan shows ascites, skin oedema and a raised middle cerebral artery peak velocity. What is the mechanism of the fetal findings?
options: Immune-mediated haemolysis of fetal red cells by maternal anti-D antibodies
Viral myocarditis causing complete heart block
Viral destruction of red cell precursors causing fetal anaemia and hydrops
Viral hepatitis causing hypoalbuminaemic oedema
questions.explain: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitors, causing fetal anaemia (raised MCA velocity) and high-output hydrops; treatment is intrauterine transfusion. Rhesus disease also gives anaemia and hydrops but follows sensitisation, not a febrile rash illness.
questions.note: Parvovirus B19 → fetal anaemia and hydrops; HBV in infants → up to 90% carriers.

questions.stem: A mother develops a chickenpox rash 2 days before delivery. Her term baby is well at birth. What is the most appropriate step for the baby?
options: Give live varicella vaccine to the baby
Give varicella-zoster immunoglobulin to the baby
Reassure; maternal antibodies will protect the baby
Separate mother and baby until a VZV PCR is negative
questions.explain: Maternal chickenpox from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery gives the baby virus without protective maternal IgG, risking severe neonatal varicella, so VZIG is given. Live vaccine is not used in neonates.
questions.note: HIV → ART, no breastfeeding; peripartum chickenpox → VZIG; no fetal scalp electrodes in HIV/HCV.

questions.stem: Which infections are part of routine antenatal screening of every pregnant woman according to standard practice?
options: HIV, CMV and toxoplasmosis
Hepatitis C, CMV and syphilis
Toxoplasmosis, rubella and HSV
HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis
questions.explain: Routine antenatal screening covers HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis, together with maternal GBS status where screening is practised. CMV and toxoplasmosis are not universally screened.
questions.note: Antenatal screening: HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis; maternal GBS status.

cards.front: Classify perinatal infections by route of transmission with examples.
cards.back: Transplacental: TORCH, parvovirus B19, VZV, Zika • intrapartum: GBS, E. coli, HSV, HBV, HIV, gonococcus, chlamydia • postnatal: NICU lines/hands (CoNS, S. aureus, Candida), breast milk, contacts.

cards.front: Give the treatment/prophylaxis for each key perinatal infection.
cards.back: HBV: vaccine + HBIG <12 h, breastfeed OK • HSV: IV aciclovir • gonococcus: ceftriaxone • chlamydia: azithromycin • GBS: penicillin G • HIV: ART, no breastfeeding • peripartum VZV: VZIG.

cards.front: How do you tell neonatal conjunctivitis causes apart by timing?
cards.back: Chemical (silver nitrate): first day • gonococcal: 2-5 days, hyperpurulent • chlamydial: 5-14 days.

II-38.summary: TORCH infections cross the placenta and hit dividing fetal cells, so they share IUGR, CNS and eye damage; the exam lies in the discriminators: periventricular calcification and deafness for CMV, diffuse calcification and chorioretinitis for toxo, the cataract-deafness-PDA triad for rubella, snuffles for syphilis.

questions.stem: Which congenital infection is the commonest worldwide?
options: Toxoplasmosis
Rubella
Cytomegalovirus
Congenital Zika virus infection syndrome
questions.explain: CMV is the commonest congenital infection and a leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss. Rubella is now rare where MMR coverage is good.
questions.note: Maternal infection crossing the placenta (transplacental); CMV is the commonest; highest risk 1st trimester.

questions.stem: A newborn has microcephaly, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly and purple-blue papules over the skin. Cranial ultrasound shows periventricular calcification and he fails the newborn hearing screen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection
Congenital toxoplasmosis
Congenital rubella syndrome
Congenital Zika virus infection syndrome
questions.explain: Periventricular calcification with sensorineural hearing loss and a blueberry muffin rash points to CMV. Toxoplasmosis gives diffuse calcification with hydrocephalus and chorioretinitis; rubella also gives deafness and blueberry muffin rash but with cataract and PDA.
questions.note: CMV: blueberry muffin rash, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, periventricular calcification, hearing loss.

questions.stem: A newborn has macrocephaly, diffuse intracranial calcification and retinal scarring. The mother kept cats during pregnancy. Which additional feature is most typical of this infection?
options: Cataract
Patent ductus arteriosus
Limb hypoplasia
Chorioretinitis
questions.explain: Congenital toxoplasmosis: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and diffuse calcification. Cataract and PDA belong to rubella, limb hypoplasia to congenital varicella.
questions.note: Toxo: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, diffuse calcification; rubella: cataract, deafness, PDA.

questions.stem: An infant born to an unscreened mother develops persistent blood-stained nasal discharge at 3 weeks, followed by a peeling rash on the palms and soles. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral azithromycin
Intravenous penicillin G
Intravenous aciclovir
Pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine
questions.explain: Snuffles and a desquamating palmoplantar rash indicate early congenital syphilis, treated with penicillin G. Late signs include saber shins.
questions.note: Syphilis: penicillin G; VZV: VZIG; rubella prevented by MMR.

questions.stem: A 4-week-old baby failed the newborn hearing screen and congenital CMV is now suspected. Why will a urine CMV PCR taken today not confirm congenital infection?
options: Urine PCR is insensitive for CMV after the first week of life
Only samples taken within 21 days of birth distinguish congenital from postnatal infection
Maternal IgG antibodies transferred across the placenta interfere with PCR testing in infancy
CMV is only shed in saliva, never in urine, after 2 weeks
questions.explain: CMV can be acquired postnatally (e.g. breast milk), so a positive sample after 21 days cannot prove congenital infection; retrospective testing of the dried blood spot can help. PCR is not affected by maternal antibody.
questions.note: CMV: urine/saliva PCR within 21 days; 80-90% asymptomatic at birth → hearing and eye follow-up.

questions.stem: A 7-day-old baby has confirmed congenital CMV with microcephaly and hearing loss. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral valganciclovir for 6 weeks
Intravenous aciclovir for 21 days
No antiviral; audiology follow-up only
Oral valganciclovir for 6 months
questions.explain: Symptomatic congenital CMV is treated with valganciclovir for 6 months, which improves hearing and developmental outcome. Aciclovir is for HSV; observation alone is for asymptomatic infants (with hearing/eye follow-up).
questions.note: Symptomatic CMV: valganciclovir 6 months; toxo: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folate.

questions.stem: A woman develops chickenpox at 13 weeks of gestation. If the fetus is affected, which pattern of abnormality is most characteristic?
options: Cicatricial skin scarring with limb hypoplasia
Hydrops fetalis from severe fetal anaemia
Cataract, deafness and patent ductus arteriosus
Periventricular calcification and hearing loss
questions.explain: First-half-of-pregnancy VZV causes congenital varicella syndrome: dermatomal scarring, limb hypoplasia, eye and CNS lesions. Hydrops is parvovirus B19; the triad is rubella; periventricular calcification is CMV.
questions.note: Parvovirus B19 → hydrops fetalis; VZV → congenital varicella syndrome (limb hypoplasia).

questions.stem: A woman with recurrent genital herpes reaches 36 weeks of gestation. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Elective caesarean section at 39 weeks regardless of lesions
Vaginal delivery with neonatal IV aciclovir for every baby
Start suppressive aciclovir now; caesarean section if lesions are present in labour
No action now; give aciclovir only if a lesion appears in labour
questions.explain: Aciclovir from 36 weeks reduces recurrences and shedding, and caesarean section is offered if active lesions are present in labour. Routine caesarean regardless of lesions or empirical treatment of all babies are not recommended.
questions.note: HSV lesions in labour: C-section; acyclovir from 36 weeks.

cards.front: Give the key discriminating signs of each TORCH infection.
cards.back: CMV: periventricular calcification, hearing loss, blueberry muffin • toxo: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, diffuse calcification • rubella: cataract, deafness, PDA • syphilis: snuffles, desquamating rash, saber shins • VZV: limb hypoplasia • B19: hydrops.

cards.front: How do you diagnose and follow up congenital CMV?
cards.back: Urine/saliva PCR within 21 days of birth • 80-90% asymptomatic at birth → hearing and eye follow-up • symptomatic: valganciclovir 6 months.

cards.front: Treatment/prevention of each TORCH infection?
cards.back: CMV: valganciclovir 6 mo • toxo: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folate • syphilis: penicillin G • VZV: VZIG • rubella: prevented by MMR • HSV: aciclovir from 36 wk, C-section if lesions.

II-39.summary: Neonatal sepsis is split at 72 hours: early-onset is vertical (GBS, E. coli, Listeria) and late-onset is nosocomial (CoNS from lines); signs are subtle, so any unwell neonate gets cultures and ampicillin plus gentamicin within an hour, swapping to cefotaxime if meningitis.

questions.stem: According to the conventional definition, what separates early-onset from late-onset neonatal sepsis?
options: Onset before versus after 7 days of life, reflecting term versus preterm birth
Onset before versus after 24 hours of life, reflecting bacterial versus viral cause
Onset before versus after 28 days of life, reflecting maternal versus community source
Onset before versus after 72 hours of life, reflecting vertical versus nosocomial acquisition
questions.explain: Early-onset (<72 h) is acquired vertically from the maternal genital tract; late-onset (>72 h) is nosocomial or community-acquired. Some GBS definitions use 7 days, but the 72-hour split reflects the route.
questions.note: Early-onset (<72 hours) = vertical; late-onset (>72 h) = nosocomial/community.

questions.stem: A 26-week preterm baby on day 12, with a long line for parenteral nutrition, develops apnoeas and temperature instability. What is the most likely organism?
options: Group B streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae)
Coagulase-negative staphylococcus
Listeria monocytogenes
Escherichia coli
questions.explain: Late-onset sepsis in a baby with a central line is most often CoNS. GBS, Listeria and E. coli are the classic early-onset vertical organisms (GBS can also cause late-onset disease, but not line sepsis).
questions.note: Late: coagulase-negative staphylococci (lines), Staph aureus, Gram-negatives, Candida.

questions.stem: A baby born at 35 weeks after membranes ruptured 30 hours before delivery, with maternal fever of 38.6 °C in labour, is grunting at 4 hours. Which group of organisms must empirical treatment cover?
options: CoNS, Staph aureus and Candida
Pseudomonas, Klebsiella and Enterococcus
GBS, E. coli and Listeria
Pneumococcus, Haemophilus and meningococcus
questions.explain: Prolonged ROM and chorioamnionitis are early-onset risks; the vertical pathogens are GBS, E. coli and Listeria, covered by ampicillin plus gentamicin. CoNS/Candida are late-onset nosocomial organisms.
questions.note: Early: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; risks: prolonged ROM, chorioamnionitis, prematurity.

questions.stem: A 5-day-old term baby is brought in because she has been feeding poorly and "seems floppy". Temperature is 35.8 °C, skin is mottled and she had a brief apnoea in triage. What is the best interpretation?
options: Probable sepsis; neonatal sepsis often presents with hypothermia and subtle signs
Probable environmental hypothermia; rewarm and observe
Probable hypoglycaemia only; feed and recheck glucose
Probable gastro-oesophageal reflux with apnoea; thicken feeds, add an alginate and discharge home
questions.explain: Neonatal sepsis is subtle: apnoea, temperature instability (often low), poor feeding and mottling. Fever is frequently absent, so these signs mandate a septic screen and antibiotics.
questions.note: Subtle: apnoea, temperature instability, grunting, poor feeding, mottling.

questions.stem: Which feature of the neonatal immune system most explains why sepsis spreads so rapidly?
options: A small neutrophil storage pool with low complement and immunoglobulin levels
An excess of maternal IgM antibodies blocking opsonisation
Overactive T-cell responses causing early cytokine storm
Absent splenic and lymph node function until the end of the first year of life
questions.explain: Neonates have small neutrophil reserves that are quickly exhausted, plus low complement and IgG (especially preterms), and invasive lines breach skin. IgM does not cross the placenta.
questions.note: Small neutrophil reserve, low complement/Ig + lines breaching skin → rapid spread.

questions.stem: A 1-day-old baby with suspected early-onset sepsis has a normal lumbar puncture. What is the recommended empirical regimen and timing?
options: Ampicillin plus cefotaxime within 1 hour
Vancomycin plus meropenem within 4 hours
Ampicillin plus gentamicin within 1 hour
Flucloxacillin plus gentamicin within 4 hours
questions.explain: Without meningitis, ampicillin plus gentamicin within the first hour covers GBS, E. coli and Listeria. Cefotaxime replaces gentamicin when meningitis is present because aminoglycosides penetrate CSF poorly.
questions.note: Without meningitis: ampicillin + gentamicin within 1 hour; with meningitis: ampicillin + cefotaxime.

questions.stem: A woman with GBS bacteriuria is in established labour and received the first dose of intrapartum penicillin G 90 minutes before a rapid delivery. Her baby is well. Which statement is correct?
options: Prophylaxis was adequate because any dose before delivery suffices
Prophylaxis was inadequate because it requires at least 4 hours before delivery
Prophylaxis was adequate and also prevents late-onset GBS disease
Prophylaxis was inadequate because only intrapartum vancomycin is effective
questions.explain: Intrapartum penicillin G must be given at least 4 hours before delivery to count as adequate; the baby needs closer observation. Even adequate prophylaxis does not prevent late-onset GBS disease.
questions.note: Prevention: intrapartum penicillin G at least 4 hours before delivery; not late-onset GBS.

questions.stem: A woman whose first baby had invasive GBS sepsis is now pregnant again and her vaginal-rectal swab at 36 weeks is GBS-negative. What is the correct plan?
options: No prophylaxis because the swab is negative
Repeat the swab at 38 weeks and decide then
Treat the mother with oral penicillin at 36 weeks only
Give intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis anyway
questions.explain: A previous baby with invasive GBS disease is an indication for intrapartum prophylaxis in every subsequent pregnancy regardless of swab result. Antenatal oral treatment does not prevent recolonisation.
questions.note: Prior invasive GBS baby → prophylaxis in every subsequent pregnancy.

cards.front: Compare early- and late-onset neonatal sepsis.
cards.back: Early <72 h, vertical: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; risks prolonged ROM, chorioamnionitis, prematurity • late >72 h, nosocomial/community: CoNS (lines), S. aureus, Gram-negatives, Candida.

cards.front: What is the empirical treatment of neonatal sepsis?
cards.back: Blood culture, CRP (serial), LP • no meningitis: ampicillin + gentamicin within 1 h • meningitis: ampicillin + cefotaxime.

cards.front: Describe GBS prevention.
cards.back: Maternal vaginal(-rectal) screening • intrapartum penicillin G ≥4 h before delivery • does not prevent late-onset GBS • prior invasive GBS baby → prophylaxis in every later pregnancy.

II-40.summary: Neonatal brain injury splits by gestation: preterms bleed (germinal matrix IVH in the first 72 hours) and get watershed PVL leading to spastic diplegia, while term babies suffer HIE, stroke and birth trauma; seizures are subtle, so check glucose and calcium first and give phenobarbital.

questions.stem: Which pair of brain injuries is characteristic of the preterm rather than the term neonate?
options: Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy and perinatal stroke
Kernicterus and subgaleal haemorrhage
Intraventricular haemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia
Perinatal arterial stroke and periventricular leukomalacia
questions.explain: IVH and PVL are preterm lesions related to the germinal matrix and watershed white matter. HIE, stroke, kernicterus and birth trauma predominate in term babies.
questions.note: Preterm: IVH and PVL; term: HIE, stroke, infection, kernicterus, birth trauma.

questions.stem: A 27-week preterm baby is being ventilated. When is intraventricular haemorrhage most likely to occur?
options: Within the first 72 hours of life
Between days 7 and 14 of life
At around 36 weeks postmenstrual age
After the first week, once feeds are established
questions.explain: IVH occurs in preterms below 32 weeks, mostly within 72 hours, as the fragile germinal matrix is exposed to fluctuating cerebral blood flow. PVL cysts appear later, after weeks.
questions.note: IVH: preterm <32 weeks, within 72 hours; HIE = commonest seizure cause.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old baby born by vacuum extraction becomes pale and tachycardic with falling haemoglobin. There is a boggy fluctuant swelling extending from the forehead to the nape that crosses the suture lines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Cephalhaematoma
Caput succedaneum
Intraventricular haemorrhage
Subgaleal haemorrhage
questions.explain: A swelling crossing sutures with shock after ventouse indicates subgaleal haemorrhage, a large potential space that can hold much of the blood volume. Cephalhaematoma is limited by sutures; caput is oedema present at birth without shock.
questions.note: Scalp swelling crossing sutures + shock → subgaleal haemorrhage; Erb palsy: waiter's tip.

questions.stem: After a difficult delivery with shoulder dystocia, a baby holds the right arm adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended and the wrist flexed; the grasp reflex is present. What is the underlying lesion?
options: Lower brachial plexus (C8-T1) injury from arm hyperabduction
Upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury from lateral neck traction
Fractured clavicle with pseudoparalysis
Radial nerve injury from humeral shaft fracture
questions.explain: The waiter's tip posture with preserved grasp is Erb palsy (C5-C6), from lateral traction on the head at delivery. Klumpke (C8-T1) affects the hand and loses the grasp; clavicle fracture gives pain-related pseudoparalysis without this posture.
questions.note: Scalp swelling crossing sutures + shock → subgaleal haemorrhage; Erb palsy: waiter's tip.

questions.stem: A former 28-week preterm develops scissoring of the legs and toe walking at 18 months, with normal arm function. Which neonatal process best explains this?
options: Germinal matrix haemorrhage extending into the ventricles
Periventricular leukomalacia from watershed white matter ischaemia
Bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia
Hypoxic-ischaemic injury to the cerebral cortex
questions.explain: PVL damages periventricular white matter where the leg fibres of the corticospinal tract run closest to the ventricles, causing spastic diplegia. Kernicterus causes dyskinetic CP; cortical HIE gives quadriplegia.
questions.note: Watershed white matter ischaemia → PVL → spastic diplegia.

questions.stem: A preterm infant's cranial ultrasound shows intraventricular blood with an echodense lesion in the adjacent periventricular parenchyma. How is this classified on the Papile scale?
options: Grade I: germinal matrix haemorrhage only
Grade II: intraventricular blood without dilatation
Grade III: intraventricular blood with ventricular dilatation
Grade IV: periventricular haemorrhagic infarction
questions.explain: Parenchymal involvement is grade IV, now understood as periventricular haemorrhagic venous infarction, with the highest risk of hemiplegia. Grades I-III are confined to the germinal matrix and ventricles.
questions.note: Cranial ultrasound; Papile I-IV; grade IV = periventricular haemorrhagic infarction.

questions.stem: A term baby has rhythmic lip smacking and cycling leg movements at 14 hours. What should be checked first?
options: Blood glucose and calcium
MRI of the brain
Serum magnesium and sodium
Lumbar puncture
questions.explain: Neonatal seizures are subtle; the first step is to exclude rapidly correctable causes: glucose and calcium, then sodium, magnesium and infection, with EEG confirmation. HIE is the commonest cause overall.
questions.note: Seizures: check glucose and calcium first, then sodium, magnesium, infection; EEG.

questions.stem: A term baby with HIE has EEG-confirmed seizures; glucose, calcium and electrolytes are normal. What is the first-line anticonvulsant?
options: Intravenous lorazepam infusion
Levetiracetam
Phenobarbital
Phenytoin
questions.explain: Phenobarbital remains first line for neonatal seizures; levetiracetam and phenytoin are second-line options. Benzodiazepines are used acutely in older children but are not first line here.
questions.note: Seizures: phenobarbital first line.

cards.front: How can you prevent IVH in a preterm baby?
cards.back: Antenatal steroids • magnesium sulphate • delayed cord clamping • avoid swings in BP and CO2 • minimal handling.

cards.front: Work up a neonatal seizure.
cards.back: Subtle signs • first: glucose and calcium • then sodium, magnesium, infection (LP) • EEG • commonest cause HIE • treatment: phenobarbital first line.

cards.front: Compare Erb and Klumpke palsy.
cards.back: Erb C5-C6: lateral traction, waiter's tip, grasp preserved • Klumpke C8-T1: hand weakness/claw, lost grasp, ± Horner • ~80% resolve spontaneously within 3 months.

II-41.summary: Most newborn skin findings are benign and need only reassurance; the skill is spotting the few that are not (SSSS, HSV, omphalitis, a problem haemangioma) and reading the umbilicus: what leaks out tells you the remnant, and a cord still attached after 3 weeks with neutrophilia means leukocyte adhesion deficiency.

questions.stem: A healthy 2-day-old term baby has blotchy erythematous macules with central yellow-white papules and pustules on the trunk, sparing the palms and soles. A smear of a pustule would most likely show what?
options: Numerous neutrophils with Gram-positive cocci
Multinucleated giant cells
Budding yeasts and pseudohyphae
Numerous eosinophils with no organisms
questions.explain: Erythema toxicum neonatorum consists of sterile pustules full of eosinophils and needs only reassurance. Neutrophils with cocci suggest impetigo; giant cells suggest HSV; yeasts suggest candida.
questions.note: Erythema toxicum: sterile pustules full of eosinophils; miliaria: sweat-duct blockage with heat.

questions.stem: A 10-day-old baby is irritable, febrile and has widespread tender erythema with large flaccid bullae; gentle rubbing shears off the epidermis, but the mouth and conjunctivae are normal. Why are the mucous membranes spared?
options: The exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein-3, which is scarce in mucosa
The exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein-1, which is scarce in mucosa
The causative streptococcal toxin cannot reach the mucosal surface
IgG autoantibodies target only keratinised epithelium
questions.explain: SSSS toxin cleaves desmoglein-1 in the granular layer; mucosa relies on desmoglein-3, so it is spared (unlike TEN). It is staphylococcal, not streptococcal, and not autoimmune.
questions.note: SSSS: exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein-1 → mucosa spared.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate treatment for the baby with staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome described above?
options: Topical fusidic acid alone
Intravenous aciclovir
Intravenous flucloxacillin
High-dose oral prednisolone
questions.explain: SSSS requires IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (flucloxacillin) plus fluids and skin care. Topical treatment is insufficient; steroids are not indicated.
questions.note: SSSS → IV flucloxacillin; omphalitis → IV antibiotics; HSV → aciclovir.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old has a clear fluid leak from the umbilicus that smells of urine and increases when he cries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Patent urachus
Patent vitelline duct
Umbilical granuloma
Omphalitis
questions.explain: Urine from the navel indicates a patent urachus (bladder-umbilicus remnant). Faeces would indicate a vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct; a granuloma is a soft moist pink nodule.
questions.note: Urine at navel = patent urachus; faeces = vitelline duct; granuloma: soft, moist, pink.

questions.stem: A 4-week-old still has the umbilical cord attached. He had an omphalitis that did not form pus, and his WBC is 45 × 10⁹/L with neutrophilia. Which test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Flow cytometry for CD18 expression on leukocytes
Dihydrorhodamine test of neutrophil oxidative burst
Serum immunoglobulin levels
Bone marrow aspirate for neutrophil precursors
questions.explain: Delayed cord separation (normally 5-15 days) with neutrophilia and pus-free infections indicates leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1, a CD18 integrin defect. DHR testing is for chronic granulomatous disease, where cord separation is normal.
questions.note: Cord separates at 5-15 days; delayed + neutrophilia → leukocyte adhesion deficiency (CD18).

questions.stem: A 6-week-old has a rapidly growing bright red raised haemangioma on the upper eyelid that is starting to close the eye. What is the best management?
options: Reassure; it will involute by school age
Surgical excision as soon as possible
Start oral propranolol
Pulsed-dye laser once growth has stopped
questions.explain: Infantile haemangiomas grow then regress, but periocular lesions threaten amblyopia, so propranolol is indicated (also for airway or ulcerated lesions). Reassurance is for uncomplicated lesions.
questions.note: Benign rashes → reassurance; hemangioma → propranolol if eye, airway, ulcer.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has a soft umbilical hernia 1 cm in diameter that reduces easily and has never been tender. What is the appropriate plan?
options: Elective surgical repair now
Monitor; most close spontaneously by age 5
Strapping the umbilicus with a coin
Urgent ultrasound to exclude bowel ischaemia
questions.explain: Soft reducible umbilical hernias are monitored because they usually close by around age 5; surgery is for persistence beyond that or very large defects. Strapping is ineffective.
questions.note: Granuloma → silver nitrate; umbilical hernia: monitor, resolves by age 5.

questions.stem: A newborn has a flat pink patch on the nape of the neck that blanches and becomes more prominent when crying. Which of the following best describes it?
options: A port-wine stain needing laser therapy
An infantile haemangioma needing propranolol
Dermal melanocytosis requiring safeguarding documentation
A benign naevus simplex needing no treatment
questions.explain: Naevus simplex (stork bite / salmon patch) is a benign capillary malformation that needs only reassurance. Dermal melanocytosis is a blue-grey lesion over the sacrum and should be documented, but it is not pink and is not abuse.
questions.note: Benign: erythema toxicum, milia, miliaria, nevus simplex, dermal melanocytosis.

cards.front: Name the umbilical discharges/lesions and their meaning.
cards.back: Urine → patent urachus • faeces → vitelline duct • soft, moist, pink nodule → granuloma (silver nitrate) • red, spreading periumbilical cellulitis → omphalitis (IV antibiotics; risk sepsis, portal vein thrombosis).

cards.front: What does delayed cord separation suggest?
cards.back: Normal separation 5-15 days • delayed + neutrophilia + infections without pus → leukocyte adhesion deficiency (CD18).

cards.front: List benign neonatal skin findings and those needing treatment.
cards.back: Benign: erythema toxicum, milia, miliaria, naevus simplex, dermal melanocytosis → reassure • treat: SSSS (IV flucloxacillin), HSV (aciclovir), omphalitis (IV antibiotics), haemangioma on eye/airway/ulcer (propranolol).

II-42.summary: NEC is the preterm on feeds whose belly distends, stools turn bloody and platelets fall; the X-ray shows pneumatosis and portal gas, and management is bowel rest, decompression and broad antibiotics with surgery for perforation. Meconium ileus is the term-baby obstruction that means cystic fibrosis until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: What is the single biggest risk factor for necrotising enterocolitis?
options: Formula feeding
Maternal chorioamnionitis
Prematurity
Umbilical arterial catheterisation
questions.explain: Prematurity is the biggest risk factor; formula feeding and poor mucosal perfusion add risk, and breast milk is protective.
questions.note: NEC: prematurity (biggest risk factor), formula feeding, abnormal flora, poor mucosal perfusion; breast milk protective.

questions.stem: A 28-week preterm baby on day 10, recently increased to full formula feeds, develops abdominal distension, large bilious gastric aspirates and fresh blood in the stool. Platelets have fallen to 60 × 10⁹/L with a metabolic acidosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Necrotising enterocolitis
Late-onset sepsis with ileus
Malrotation with midgut volvulus
Cow's milk protein allergy
questions.explain: Preterm, feeds established, distension, feed intolerance, bloody stool plus thrombocytopenia and acidosis is NEC. Volvulus is possible but less likely in this setting; sepsis with ileus does not usually cause bloody stools.
questions.note: NEC: abdominal distension, nutritional intolerance, bloody stool; instability, low platelets, acidosis.

questions.stem: In the baby above, which abdominal X-ray finding is pathognomonic of the diagnosis?
options: A double-bubble with no distal gas
Soap-bubble appearance in the right iliac fossa
Multiple air-fluid levels with a gasless rectum
Intramural gas (pneumatosis intestinalis)
questions.explain: Pneumatosis intestinalis (bubbles of gas in the bowel wall), with or without portal venous gas, is diagnostic of NEC. Double bubble is duodenal atresia; soap bubble is meconium ileus.
questions.note: NEC X-ray: pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas; Rigler sign = perforation.

questions.stem: A ventilated 26-week baby with NEC deteriorates and cannot safely be moved upright. Which radiograph is best for detecting a perforation, and what sign confirms it?
options: Erect chest film; air under the diaphragm
Supine horizontal-beam lateral film; gas outlining both sides of the bowel wall
Supine AP film only; branching gas in the portal venous system over the liver
Contrast enema; leak of contrast into the peritoneum
questions.explain: A horizontal (cross-table) beam with the baby lying on its back shows free air rising anteriorly; Rigler sign (gas on both sides of the bowel wall) indicates perforation. An erect film is impractical, portal gas does not mean perforation, and contrast enema is contraindicated in NEC.
questions.note: Baby cannot be moved: horizontal X-ray from side position, lying on back.

questions.stem: What is the initial management of stage II NEC without perforation?
options: Continue feeds with lactase-treated formula and oral metronidazole
Nil by mouth, NG decompression, IV fluids, TPN and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
Urgent laparotomy with resection of affected bowel
Nil by mouth and IV fluids only for 24 hours, then re-feed
questions.explain: NEC is managed medically with bowel rest, decompression, TPN and antibiotics covering Gram-negatives and anaerobes, typically for 7-14 days. Surgery is for perforation, peritonitis or deterioration despite therapy.
questions.note: NEC: NPO (bowel rest), NG decompression, IV fluids, TPN, IV antibiotics (gram-negative, anaerobes).

questions.stem: A preterm baby has been on full medical treatment for NEC for 36 hours. Which finding is an indication for surgery?
options: Persistent pneumatosis intestinalis on the repeat abdominal radiograph
Bilious aspirates still present at 36 hours
Platelet count of 90 × 10⁹/L on day 2
Progressive clinical deterioration despite maximal medical therapy
questions.explain: Surgery is indicated for perforation, peritonitis or worsening despite medical therapy. Persistent pneumatosis or aspirates alone are expected during medical management.
questions.note: Surgery for perforation, peritonitis, or worsening despite medical therapy.

questions.stem: A term newborn has abdominal distension and bilious vomiting and has not passed meconium at 36 hours. The X-ray shows dilated loops with a granular soap-bubble appearance in the right lower quadrant, and a contrast enema reveals a microcolon. What is the most likely underlying condition?
options: Cystic fibrosis
Hirschsprung disease
Hypothyroidism
Jejunal atresia
questions.explain: Meconium ileus (sticky meconium obstructing the terminal ileum) is almost always due to CF and is its earliest manifestation in about 15% of patients; confirm later with a sweat test. Hirschsprung gives a transition zone rather than microcolon with soap bubbles.
questions.note: Meconium ileus: terminal ileum blocked by sticky meconium = cystic fibrosis (~15%).

questions.stem: What is the first-line treatment of uncomplicated meconium ileus?
options: Immediate laparotomy with enterotomy and irrigation
Rectal suction biopsy followed by colostomy
Gastrografin (hyperosmolar contrast) enema, proceeding to surgery if it fails
Oral pancreatic enzyme replacement and osmotic laxatives for 48 hours, then review
questions.explain: A Gastrografin enema draws fluid into the bowel and loosens meconium; surgery follows if it fails or if there is perforation/volvulus. Rectal biopsy is for Hirschsprung disease.
questions.note: Meconium ileus: Gastrografin enema → surgery if it fails.

cards.front: List the X-ray signs of NEC and perforation.
cards.back: Pneumatosis intestinalis (diagnostic) • portal venous gas • perforation: Rigler sign (double-wall), free air on horizontal-beam film with baby supine.

cards.front: How do you manage NEC?
cards.back: NPO (bowel rest) • NG decompression • IV fluids, TPN • IV antibiotics for Gram-negatives and anaerobes • surgery for perforation, peritonitis or worsening despite medical therapy.

cards.front: Describe meconium ileus: features, X-ray and management.
cards.back: CF ~15% present this way • distension, bilious vomiting, no meconium • X-ray soap-bubble, microcolon on enema • Gastrografin enema → surgery if fails • later sweat test.

II-43.summary: CDH and oesophageal atresia are both diagnosed in the delivery room: a scaphoid abdomen with heart sounds on the right means intubate, never bag-mask; drooling and choking at the first feed mean pass an NG tube and watch it coil. CDH is a physiological emergency (pulmonary hypoplasia and hypertension), not a surgical one.

questions.stem: Where is the defect in a typical congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
options: Right anteromedial (Morgagni) defect
Left anteromedial (Morgagni) defect
Central tendon eventration
Left posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect
questions.explain: Most CDHs are left-sided posterolateral Bochdalek hernias. Morgagni hernias are anterior, usually right-sided, and present later.
questions.note: CDH: usually left-sided posterolateral Bochdalek hernia.

questions.stem: A term baby has severe respiratory distress immediately after birth. The abdomen is scaphoid, breath sounds are reduced on the left and the heart sounds are loudest on the right of the chest. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Bag-and-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen, then a chest X-ray
Intubate and pass an NG tube; avoid bag-and-mask ventilation
Insert a left-sided chest drain
Start CPAP via nasal prongs
questions.explain: This is CDH. Bag-mask ventilation inflates the herniated stomach and bowel, worsening lung compression, so intubate early and decompress with an NG tube. A chest drain risks perforating bowel in the chest.
questions.note: CDH: intubate, no bag-mask, NG tube, gentle ventilation, treat pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: In congenital diaphragmatic hernia, which factors primarily determine survival?
options: Size of the diaphragmatic defect and timing of surgery
Associated VACTERL anomalies and prematurity
Pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension
Volvulus and ischaemia of herniated bowel
questions.explain: Survival depends on how hypoplastic the lungs are and the severity of pulmonary hypertension, not on the hernia repair itself, which is why surgery is deferred until stable.
questions.note: CDH: pulmonary hypoplasia + pulmonary hypertension determine survival.

questions.stem: A baby with CDH is intubated at birth and remains hypoxic with pre/post-ductal gap of 15%. The parents ask when the surgeon will operate. What is the correct answer?
options: After cardiorespiratory stabilisation, as CDH is a physiological rather than surgical emergency
Immediately, because reducing the bowel will relieve the lung compression
Within 6 hours, before the bowel becomes ischaemic in the chest
Only after the baby has been extubated and established on feeds
questions.explain: Early surgery does not improve survival; it is performed once pulmonary hypertension and ventilation are stabilised. Waiting for extubation is not required since repair usually happens while ventilated.
questions.note: CDH surgery after stabilisation: physiological, not surgical, emergency.

questions.stem: A newborn born after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios has frothy saliva bubbling from the mouth and coughs and turns blue during the first feed. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Pass a firm wide-bore NG tube and take an X-ray
Perform a contrast swallow with barium
Arrange urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
Thicken feeds and observe for 24 hours
questions.explain: Drooling and choking at first feed with polyhydramnios suggests oesophageal atresia; a firm tube will coil in the blind pouch on X-ray. Barium risks aspiration and is not needed for diagnosis.
questions.note: OA: excess drooling, choking at first feeding; distal fistula: abdominal distension.

questions.stem: A baby with oesophageal atresia has an X-ray showing the NG tube coiled in the upper chest and a gasless abdomen. What does this indicate?
options: Oesophageal atresia with a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula
An H-type fistula without atresia
Pure oesophageal atresia with no distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Oesophageal atresia with both proximal and distal fistulae
questions.explain: Gastric gas means air reaches the stomach via a distal fistula (the commonest, 85% type); a gasless abdomen means no distal connection, i.e. pure OA (or proximal fistula only).
questions.note: Pure OA: gasless abdomen; VACTERL screen, echo.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old has had coughing and choking with every feed since birth and three episodes of right upper lobe pneumonia. An NG tube passes easily into the stomach. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
H-type tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Vascular ring compressing the oesophagus
Laryngomalacia
questions.explain: Cough since birth, always during feeds, with recurrent aspiration and a patent oesophagus suggests an H-type TEF without atresia; diagnose with prone tube oesophagogram or bronchoscopy. GORD and laryngomalacia are not specifically tied to every feed from birth.
questions.note: Cough since birth, always during feeding → H-type TEF.

questions.stem: A baby is confirmed to have oesophageal atresia with distal TEF. Before surgery, which investigations are most important given the associated anomalies?
options: Sweat test, faecal elastase and genetic testing for cystic fibrosis
Karyotype for trisomy 21 and thyroid function only
Cranial ultrasound, ophthalmology review and TORCH serology for congenital infection
Echocardiogram, renal ultrasound and spinal/limb assessment for VACTERL anomalies
questions.explain: OA/TEF is associated with VACTERL (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, TE, renal, limb) mesodermal defects; echo is also essential to locate the aortic arch before thoracotomy. A Replogle tube keeps the pouch clear meanwhile.
questions.note: CDH: abdominal viscera herniate into chest; OA/TEF: associated VACTERL anomalies (mesodermal defects).

cards.front: Delivery-room management of CDH?
cards.back: Intubate, no bag-mask • NG tube decompression • gentle ventilation • treat pulmonary hypertension • surgery only after stabilisation (physiological, not surgical, emergency).

cards.front: How do you diagnose oesophageal atresia and its type?
cards.back: Polyhydramnios, drooling, choking at first feed • firm NG tube coils in pouch on X-ray • gastric gas = distal TEF (85%) • gasless abdomen = pure OA • H-type: cough with every feed since birth.

cards.front: What does VACTERL stand for and why screen?
cards.back: Vertebral, Anorectal, Cardiac, Tracheo-oEsophageal, Renal, Limb • mesodermal defects associated with OA/TEF • echo, renal US, spine/limb X-rays before surgery.

II-44.summary: Bilious vomiting in a newborn is obstruction below the ampulla until proven otherwise: a flat abdomen with a double bubble is duodenal atresia (think Down syndrome, exclude malrotation), many distended loops is jejunoileal atresia. For wall defects: a membrane-covered midline sac (omphalocele) brings syndromes; bare bowel right of the cord (gastroschisis) brings young mothers and is otherwise isolated.

questions.stem: Which condition is most strongly associated with duodenal atresia?
options: Trisomy 18
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
Trisomy 21
Cystic fibrosis
questions.explain: Duodenal atresia results from failed recanalisation and is classically associated with Down syndrome (about 30%). Trisomy 18 and Beckwith-Wiedemann are associated with omphalocele; CF with meconium ileus.
questions.note: Duodenal: failed recanalisation, trisomy 21; jejunoileal: in-utero vascular accident.

questions.stem: A newborn with upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease has bilious vomiting from the first feed. The abdomen is flat and soft. What would the abdominal X-ray most likely show?
options: A double bubble with no distal bowel gas
Multiple dilated loops with air-fluid levels
Pneumatosis intestinalis
A soap-bubble appearance with microcolon
questions.explain: Down syndrome, bilious vomiting from the first feed and a flat abdomen suggest duodenal atresia: gas in stomach and duodenum (double bubble) with nothing beyond. Many dilated loops would indicate a lower (jejunoileal) atresia.
questions.note: Duodenal atresia: double bubble on abdominal X-ray; exclude malrotation.

questions.stem: Why does duodenal atresia usually cause bilious rather than non-bilious vomiting, and which antenatal finding often accompanies it?
options: The obstruction lies proximal to the ampulla of Vater; oligohydramnios
Bile refluxes through a patent pylorus; oligohydramnios
The obstruction lies distal to the ampulla of Vater; oligohydramnios
The obstruction lies distal to the ampulla of Vater; polyhydramnios
questions.explain: Most duodenal atresias are below the ampulla, so vomit contains bile from the first feed; the fetus cannot absorb swallowed amniotic fluid, causing polyhydramnios.
questions.note: Obstruction below ampulla → bilious vomiting from first feed, polyhydramnios.

questions.stem: A newborn has bilious vomiting on day 1 and a progressively distended abdomen; the X-ray shows many dilated small-bowel loops with air-fluid levels. Which mechanism is most likely responsible?
options: Failure of recanalisation of the bowel lumen
An in-utero mesenteric vascular accident
Absent ganglion cells in the distal colon
Sticky meconium obstructing the terminal ileum
questions.explain: Jejunoileal atresia follows an in-utero vascular accident and causes distension with many loops. Failed recanalisation is the mechanism of duodenal atresia (flat abdomen).
questions.note: Duodenal: bilious vomiting, flat abdomen; jejunoileal: distension, many loops.

questions.stem: A newborn has a full-thickness abdominal wall defect to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord with uncovered, thickened bowel loops. Which statement is most accurate?
options: It is usually associated with trisomy 13 or 18
It is usually isolated and is associated with young maternal age
It is typically part of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
It is usually accompanied by major cardiac malformations
questions.explain: This is gastroschisis: right of the cord, no membrane, associated with young mothers and rarely with other anomalies (apart from bowel atresia). Omphalocele is midline, sac-covered and associated with trisomies, BWS and cardiac/GU/neural tube defects.
questions.note: Omphalocele: midline, covered by sac; gastroschisis: right of cord, no membrane.

questions.stem: A newborn with a midline membrane-covered abdominal wall defect containing liver and bowel also has macroglossia and hypoglycaemia. What is the most likely underlying syndrome?
options: Trisomy 21
Prader-Willi syndrome
Congenital hypothyroidism
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
questions.explain: Omphalocele plus macroglossia and neonatal hypoglycaemia (from hyperinsulinism) is Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome; trisomies 13 and 18 are the other classic associations. Hypothyroidism gives macroglossia and umbilical hernia but not omphalocele.
questions.note: Omphalocele: Beckwith-Wiedemann, trisomies 13, 18; gastroschisis: young mothers.

questions.stem: A baby with gastroschisis is born in your unit. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Cover bowel in sterile saline dressings or a bag, insert an NG tube, give IV fluids
Reduce the bowel manually into the abdomen at the bedside
Leave the bowel exposed to the air and start early oral feeds to promote gut motility
Apply a dry compression bandage and arrange elective repair at 6 weeks
questions.explain: Exposed bowel loses heat and fluid, so it is covered with sterile saline dressings/cling bag, decompressed with an NG tube and the baby given fluids; then primary closure or a staged silo repair. Forceful bedside reduction risks abdominal compartment syndrome.
questions.note: Wrap bowel in sterile saline dressings, NG tube; primary closure, else staged silo repair.

questions.stem: A newborn boy has no anal opening; the invertogram/perineal ultrasound shows the rectal pouch ending high above the levator ani with no perineal fistula. What is the initial surgical management?
options: Primary perineal anoplasty within the first 24 hours of life, no stoma
Serial anal dilatation from day 2
Diverting colostomy, then posterior sagittal anorectoplasty later
Gastrografin enema to clear the obstruction
questions.explain: High anal atresia is managed with an initial colostomy followed by PSARP; low lesions (e.g. perineal fistula) can have a primary anoplasty. Dilatation and enemas have no role in an atretic anus.
questions.note: High anal atresia: colostomy → PSARP; low → anoplasty.

cards.front: Compare omphalocele and gastroschisis.
cards.back: Omphalocele: midline, sac-covered, cord inserts into sac; BWS, trisomy 13/18; cardiac, GU, neural tube defects • gastroschisis: right of cord, no membrane, young mothers, usually isolated.

cards.front: Duodenal vs jejunoileal atresia.
cards.back: Duodenal: failed recanalisation, trisomy 21, bilious vomiting, flat abdomen, double bubble, exclude malrotation → duodenoduodenostomy • jejunoileal: in-utero vascular accident, distension, many loops.

cards.front: Management of abdominal wall defects and anal atresia.
cards.back: Sterile saline dressings, NG tube, IV fluids → primary closure or staged silo • high anal atresia: colostomy → PSARP • low: anoplasty.

II-45.summary: Following up a preterm means BPD (still needing oxygen or support at 36 weeks PMA), ROP screening (<31 weeks or <1501 g), corrected age for growth and development but chronological age for vaccines, plus iron, vitamin D and RSV prophylaxis.

questions.stem: How is bronchopulmonary dysplasia defined?
options: Need for oxygen at 28 days of life regardless of gestation
Need for mechanical ventilation beyond 7 days of life
Need for oxygen at discharge home at any gestation
Need for oxygen or respiratory support at 36 weeks postmenstrual age
questions.explain: BPD is defined by oxygen or respiratory support at 36 weeks PMA; oxygen need at 28 days was the older definition and is still part of severity grading.
questions.note: BPD = oxygen or respiratory support at 36 weeks PMA.

questions.stem: A 25-week baby was ventilated for 3 weeks with high oxygen requirements and had an episode of sepsis. Which combination of factors best explains his development of BPD?
options: Surfactant therapy with caffeine and antenatal steroids
Prematurity with oxygen toxicity, ventilator trauma and infection
Meconium aspiration with persistent pulmonary hypertension
Congenital surfactant protein B deficiency
questions.explain: BPD results from prematurity plus oxygen toxicity, volutrauma/barotrauma and infection. Surfactant, caffeine and antenatal steroids are preventive.
questions.note: Prematurity plus oxygen toxicity (RIB), ventilator trauma, infection.

questions.stem: An ex-24-week infant with BPD has rising oxygen requirements at 4 months. What is the underlying lung pathology of modern ('new') BPD, and which complication should be sought?
options: Recurrent aspiration pneumonitis; bronchiectasis
Hyaline membrane formation; pneumothorax
Arrested alveolar and vascular development; pulmonary hypertension
Excess surfactant production; alveolar proteinosis
questions.explain: Modern BPD is arrested alveolarisation and vascular growth giving fewer, simplified alveoli, with a risk of pulmonary hypertension; rising oxygen needs should prompt an echo.
questions.note: BPD: arrested alveolar/vascular growth + injury → simplified alveoli, pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A baby born at 30 weeks weighing 1650 g is now 4 weeks old. Does he meet ROP screening criteria?
options: Yes, because he was born before 31 weeks
No, because his birthweight is above 1500 g
No, because screening is only for babies under 28 weeks
Yes, but only if he received supplemental oxygen
questions.explain: ROP screening is offered to babies born <31 weeks OR <1501 g; meeting either criterion qualifies. Oxygen exposure is not a requirement.
questions.note: ROP screen: <31 weeks or <1501 g; BPD with rising O2 → echo.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes the pathogenesis of retinopathy of prematurity?
options: Hyperoxia halts vessel growth; the avascular retina turns hypoxic, VEGF surges and neovessels grow
Low oxygen causes recurrent retinal haemorrhages, which organise into fibrous scar tissue and detach the retina
High oxygen directly damages photoreceptors, causing retinal detachment
Infection of the retina by maternal organisms causes vasculitis and scarring
questions.explain: Relative hyperoxia suppresses VEGF and halts vascularisation; the peripheral avascular retina then becomes hypoxic, VEGF surges, and abnormal neovessels grow, which may lead to detachment.
questions.note: ROP: high oxygen → hypoxic retina → VEGF surge → neovascularisation.

questions.stem: A baby born at 28 weeks is now 6 months old. At what corrected age should his development be assessed, and how should his vaccines be timed?
options: Development at 6 months; vaccines delayed to corrected age
Development at 3 months corrected; vaccines delayed to corrected age
Development at 3 months corrected; vaccines at chronological age
Development at 6 months; vaccines at chronological age
questions.explain: Born 12 weeks early, he is 3 months corrected; correct for prematurity until about 2 years for growth and development. Vaccines are given by chronological age, without delay.
questions.note: Corrected age for growth/development (~2 years); chronological for vaccines.

questions.stem: A former 27-week infant is being discharged in October. Which supplements and preventive measure are recommended?
options: Vitamin K and folic acid supplements plus BCG vaccination
Iron and vitamin D supplements plus RSV prophylaxis with nirsevimab or palivizumab
Iron and calcium supplements plus influenza vaccination at birth
Vitamin D alone plus oral azithromycin prophylaxis throughout the winter RSV season
questions.explain: Preterm infants have low iron stores and vitamin D needs, and are at high risk of severe RSV; nirsevimab (or palivizumab) is given for the RSV season.
questions.note: Supplement iron, vitamin D; RSV prevention: nirsevimab or palivizumab.

questions.stem: ROP screening of a 34-week-PMA infant shows stage 3 disease with plus disease in zone II (treatment-requiring ROP). What is the appropriate management?
options: Increase oxygen saturation targets to above 98%
Repeat screening in 2 weeks and treat if progressing
Topical corticosteroid eye drops
Laser photocoagulation or intravitreal anti-VEGF injection
questions.explain: Treatment-requiring ROP is treated with laser ablation of avascular retina or anti-VEGF (e.g. bevacizumab/ranibizumab). Waiting risks retinal detachment; high oxygen is not therapeutic.
questions.note: ROP: laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF.

cards.front: Define BPD and list prevention strategies.
cards.back: O2 or respiratory support at 36 weeks PMA • prevention: maternal glucocorticoids, surfactant, caffeine, gentle ventilation, avoid hyperoxia, nutrition.

cards.front: What should follow-up of a preterm baby include?
cards.back: Growth and neurodevelopment by corrected age (~2 y) • PVL → spastic diplegia • hearing • vision/ROP • vaccines by chronological age • iron, vitamin D • RSV prophylaxis (nirsevimab/palivizumab).

cards.front: ROP: screening criteria, mechanism and treatment.
cards.back: Screen <31 weeks or <1501 g • high O2 → hypoxic retina → VEGF surge → neovascularisation • laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF.

II-46.summary: Hodgkin is the adolescent with painless rubbery neck nodes, B symptoms and Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15/CD30), cured in more than 90%; childhood NHL is high grade and fast, meaning tumour lysis (Burkitt) and mediastinal airway compromise (lymphoblastic). Biopsy before steroids and never lie a mediastinal mass flat under GA.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl has a 3-month history of a painless, rubbery 3 cm left supraclavicular node, night sweats that soak her sheets and 12% weight loss. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Fine-needle aspiration cytology
Trial of antibiotics and review in 2 weeks
Excision biopsy of the lymph node
Epstein-Barr virus serology only
questions.explain: A persistent, >2 cm supraclavicular node with B symptoms is suspicious for Hodgkin lymphoma; excision biopsy is needed to see nodal architecture and Reed-Sternberg cells. FNA is inadequate for lymphoma diagnosis.
questions.note: Suspicious node: >2 cm, hard, supraclavicular, persistent.

questions.stem: Which immunophenotype is characteristic of Reed-Sternberg cells in classical Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: CD15 and CD30 positive
CD19 and CD20 positive
CD3 and CD7 positive
CD10 and TdT positive
questions.explain: Classical RS cells express CD15 and CD30 (and usually lack CD45). TdT/CD10 are lymphoblastic markers; CD3/CD7 are T-cell markers.
questions.note: Excision biopsy: RS cells CD15, CD30; CXR, PET-CT; staging predicts prognosis.

questions.stem: Which subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma is commonest in adolescents?
options: Mixed cellularity
Lymphocyte-depleted
Nodular lymphocyte-predominant
Nodular sclerosis
questions.explain: Nodular sclerosis accounts for about 70% of cases and typically involves the mediastinum and neck in adolescents. Mixed cellularity is more common in younger children and in low-income settings.
questions.note: Hodgkin: nodular sclerosis commonest (70%).

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy has a rapidly enlarging right iliac fossa mass over 2 weeks. Biopsy shows a 'starry sky' pattern with a very high proliferation index. Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
options: t(9;22) BCR-ABL1
t(8;14) involving MYC
t(12;21) ETV6-RUNX1
t(2;5) NPM-ALK
questions.explain: Burkitt lymphoma presents as an abdominal mass with a starry-sky pattern and t(8;14) MYC translocation. ETV6-RUNX1 is a favourable ALL marker; NPM-ALK is anaplastic large cell lymphoma.
questions.note: NHL: Burkitt t(8;14) MYC, lymphoblastic, DLBCL, ALCL.

questions.stem: Twelve hours after starting chemotherapy for Burkitt lymphoma, a boy has reduced urine output and develops muscle cramps. Which biochemical pattern is expected?
options: Low potassium, low phosphate, high urate and high calcium
High potassium, high phosphate, high urate and low calcium
High potassium, low phosphate, low urate and high calcium
Low sodium, high phosphate, low urate and low calcium
questions.explain: Tumour lysis releases intracellular K, phosphate and nucleic acids (urate); phosphate precipitates calcium, causing hypocalcaemia (cramps, tetany). Burkitt is the classic high-risk tumour.
questions.note: Burkitt lysis → TLS: high K, phosphate, urate, low calcium.

questions.stem: A boy with Burkitt lymphoma at high risk of tumour lysis is found to have G6PD deficiency. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Hyperhydration with rasburicase at standard dose
Rasburicase with urinary alkalinisation
Fluid restriction with oral phosphate binders only
Hyperhydration with allopurinol rather than rasburicase
questions.explain: Rasburicase produces hydrogen peroxide and can cause severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in G6PD deficiency, so allopurinol is used instead with hyperhydration. Fluid restriction would worsen TLS.
questions.note: TLS: hyperhydrate, rasburicase (contraindicated in G6PD deficiency).

questions.stem: A 13-year-old with a large anterior mediastinal mass, orthopnoea and stridor is booked for a biopsy. What is the key safety consideration?
options: Avoid general anaesthesia and lying flat; biopsy under local anaesthesia if possible
Give high-dose dexamethasone first to shrink the mass before attempting any tissue biopsy
Perform the biopsy under general anaesthesia with muscle relaxation
Insert a central line under general anaesthesia before staging
questions.explain: Lying flat or GA with relaxation can cause complete airway or cardiovascular collapse from a mediastinal mass. Steroids before biopsy can destroy the diagnosis (lymphoblastic lymphoma/ALL), so they are avoided unless life-threatening.
questions.note: Mediastinal mass → avoid general anaesthesia and lying flat.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with cervical lymphadenopathy and a mediastinal mass on CXR is seen by a GP who suspects asthma and wants to start oral prednisolone for wheeze. Why is this dangerous?
options: Steroids precipitate Pneumocystis pneumonia in mediastinal disease
Steroids worsen superior vena cava obstruction by fluid retention
Steroids can lyse lymphoma cells and obscure the diagnosis before biopsy
Steroids cause rapid regrowth of Hodgkin disease once stopped
questions.explain: Lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukaemia is exquisitely steroid-sensitive; pre-biopsy steroids can make histology uninterpretable and trigger TLS. Hence 'no steroids before biopsy'.
questions.note: No steroids before biopsy.

cards.front: Hodgkin vs childhood NHL.
cards.back: Hodgkin: adolescents, RS cells CD15/CD30, contiguous nodal spread, B symptoms, nodular sclerosis 70%, cure >90% • NHL: high grade (Burkitt t(8;14), lymphoblastic, DLBCL, ALCL), abdominal or mediastinal mass, TLS risk.

cards.front: Which lymph node features are suspicious?
cards.back: Node >2 cm, hard/rubbery, painless, supraclavicular, persistent/enlarging, B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss >10%) → excision biopsy, no steroids before.

cards.front: Tumour lysis syndrome: labs and management.
cards.back: High K, phosphate, urate; low calcium • hyperhydrate • rasburicase (contraindicated in G6PD deficiency → allopurinol) • monitor electrolytes, dialysis if needed.

II-47.summary: ALL is the commonest childhood cancer (peak 2-5 years): blasts crowding the marrow give pallor, bruising, infection and bone pain. Diagnose with marrow, flow cytometry and genetics, risk-stratify by age, WBC, genetics and above all MRD, and remember the CNS is a sanctuary that needs intrathecal therapy.

questions.stem: What is the commonest childhood malignancy and its peak age?
options: Acute myeloid leukaemia, peak in infancy
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, peak in adolescence
Neuroblastoma, peak 2-5 years
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, peak 2-5 years
questions.explain: ALL makes up about 80% of childhood leukaemia, the commonest childhood cancer, with a peak at 2-5 years. Neuroblastoma is the commonest extracranial solid tumour, mostly under 2.
questions.note: Commonest childhood cancer; ALL ~80%, peak 2-5 years.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has 3 weeks of pallor, bruising and limping with night-time leg pain. Examination shows hepatosplenomegaly and generalised lymphadenopathy; FBC shows Hb 72 g/L, platelets 25 × 10⁹/L and WBC 3.1 × 10⁹/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Aplastic anaemia
questions.explain: Pancytopenia with bone pain, organomegaly and lymphadenopathy indicates marrow infiltration by blasts. ITP has isolated thrombocytopenia and no organomegaly; aplastic anaemia lacks organomegaly; JIA does not cause pancytopenia.
questions.note: Pallor, bleeding, infection, bone pain, HSM, lymphadenopathy; mediastinal mass in T-ALL.

questions.stem: Why is intrathecal chemotherapy an essential part of ALL treatment even when the initial CSF is clear?
options: Intrathecal drugs are needed to prevent chemotherapy-induced neuropathy
The CNS is the site where leukaemic stem cells originate
The CNS is a sanctuary site that systemic chemotherapy penetrates poorly
Systemic chemotherapy is neurotoxic and must be avoided
questions.explain: The blood-brain barrier shields leukaemic cells from most systemic drugs, so CNS-directed therapy (intrathecal methotrexate) prevents CNS relapse.
questions.note: Blasts fill marrow → anaemia, bleeding, infection; infiltration → bone pain, organomegaly; CNS a sanctuary.

questions.stem: Which congenital condition most increases the risk of childhood leukaemia?
options: Down syndrome
Turner syndrome
Marfan syndrome
Cystic fibrosis
questions.explain: Down syndrome carries a markedly increased risk of both ALL and AML (especially AMKL), and transient abnormal myelopoiesis in neonates.
questions.note: Risk factor: Down syndrome.

questions.stem: Which child with newly diagnosed B-ALL has the most favourable prognosis?
options: A 4-year-old, WBC 12 × 10⁹/L, ETV6-RUNX1 positive, MRD negative at end of induction
An 8-month-old, WBC 12 × 10⁹/L, KMT2A rearranged, MRD negative at end of induction
A 4-year-old, WBC 80 × 10⁹/L, hyperdiploid, MRD positive at end of induction
A 14-year-old, WBC 12 × 10⁹/L, ETV6-RUNX1 positive, MRD positive at end of induction
questions.explain: Good features are age 1-10, WBC <50, hyperdiploidy or ETV6-RUNX1, and above all MRD negativity, the strongest prognostic factor. Infancy (with KMT2A), age >10, high WBC and positive MRD are adverse.
questions.note: Good: age 1-10, WBC <50, hyperdiploidy/ETV6-RUNX1; minimal residual disease strongest.

questions.stem: A child with suspected leukaemia has blasts on the blood film. Which investigation set is required to confirm and classify the disease?
options: Peripheral blood film and CT chest, abdomen and pelvis
Lymph node excision biopsy with immunohistochemistry and whole-body PET-CT staging
Bone marrow examination with flow cytometry and cytogenetics, plus lumbar puncture
Bone marrow trephine alone and serum LDH
questions.explain: Marrow morphology, flow cytometry (lineage) and genetics (risk) are needed, with LP to assess CNS involvement. Excision biopsy and PET-CT are the work-up of lymphoma.
questions.note: Bone marrow examination + flow cytometry, genetics; LP.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old in ALL maintenance therapy presents with a temperature of 38.6 °C; neutrophils are 0.3 × 10⁹/L. He looks well. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral amoxicillin and review in 24 hours
Take cultures and give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
Wait for the blood culture result before starting antibiotics
Paracetamol and repeat the neutrophil count tomorrow
questions.explain: Febrile neutropenia is an emergency regardless of how well the child looks; IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam) within 1 hour. Children also receive co-trimoxazole prophylaxis against Pneumocystis.
questions.note: Febrile neutropenia → IV antibiotics within 1 hour; co-trimoxazole vs Pneumocystis.

questions.stem: A child with early bone marrow relapse of ALL undergoes an allogeneic stem cell transplant from a matched sibling. What is the main immunological mechanism by which the transplant reduces relapse beyond the conditioning chemotherapy?
options: Host T cells reject the donor graft and release cytokines that kill blasts
Donor stem cells produce antibodies that block blast proliferation
Conditioning radiotherapy permanently sterilises the CNS sanctuary
Donor T cells recognise and kill residual leukaemic cells (graft versus leukaemia)
questions.explain: Graft versus leukaemia means donor immune cells attack leukaemic cells, the basis of SCT benefit in high-risk/relapsed ALL (and linked to GvHD). Host-versus-graft is rejection, which is harmful.
questions.note: High-risk/relapse: allogeneic SCT; graft versus leukaemia = donor cells attack leukaemic cells.

cards.front: List the phases of ALL treatment.
cards.back: Induction → consolidation + intrathecal methotrexate (CNS) → intensification → maintenance (~2 years) • cure ~90% • high-risk/relapse: allogeneic SCT.

cards.front: Give the prognostic factors in childhood ALL.
cards.back: Good: age 1-10, WBC <50, hyperdiploidy or ETV6-RUNX1 • strongest: MRD after induction • poor: infant/adolescent, high WBC, T-ALL with mediastinal mass, MRD positive.

cards.front: Supportive care in leukaemia.
cards.back: Febrile neutropenia → IV antibiotics within 1 h • co-trimoxazole vs Pneumocystis • TLS prevention (hydration, rasburicase/allopurinol) • blood products.

II-48.summary: Platelet bleeding is skin and mucosa, not joints. A well child with isolated thrombocytopenia weeks after a virus is ITP: no marrow, observe if only skin signs; but anything else abnormal (other cell lines, organomegaly, bone pain) means marrow to exclude leukaemia.

questions.stem: Which bleeding pattern most suggests a platelet disorder rather than a coagulation factor deficiency?
options: Haemarthroses and deep muscle haematomas
Delayed bleeding hours after circumcision
Petechiae, purpura and epistaxis
Retroperitoneal haematoma after minor trauma
questions.explain: Platelet disorders bleed into skin and mucosa (petechiae, purpura, epistaxis). Joint and muscle bleeds and delayed bleeding are typical of haemophilia.
questions.note: Low, dysfunctional or high platelets; bleed into skin and mucosa, not joints.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old had a cold 3 weeks ago and now has widespread petechiae and bruises. She is well and active, with no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. FBC shows platelets 12 × 10⁹/L, normal Hb and WBC; the film shows large platelets. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Henoch-Schönlein purpura
questions.explain: Well child, purpura weeks after a viral illness, isolated thrombocytopenia with large platelets and no organomegaly is ITP. Leukaemia usually affects other lines or causes organomegaly; HSP has a normal platelet count.
questions.note: ITP: well child, purpura 3 weeks after viral illness, no organomegaly.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of thrombocytopenia in childhood ITP?
options: IgM antibodies against GPIb-IX cause complement lysis of platelets in the liver
Deficient ADAMTS13 causes platelet consumption in microthrombi
Viral infection of megakaryocytes suppresses marrow production
IgG antibodies against GPIIb/IIIa cause splenic macrophage clearance of platelets
questions.explain: Autoantibodies (IgG) against GPIIb/IIIa opsonise platelets, which are removed by splenic macrophages; the marrow responds with increased megakaryocytes. ADAMTS13 deficiency is TTP.
questions.note: ITP: IgG against GPIIb/IIIa → platelets consumed by splenic macrophages.

questions.stem: The child with ITP above has only cutaneous bruising and petechiae with no mucosal bleeding. What is the best management?
options: Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks, then taper
Observation only; most resolve within 6 months
Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.8-1 g/kg as a single dose
Platelet transfusion
questions.explain: With cutaneous bleeding only, observation is recommended as 75-80% resolve within 6 months. Steroids are for mucosal bleeding, IVIG for significant bleeding; platelet transfusion is for life-threatening haemorrhage only.
questions.note: ITP: cutaneous only → observation (75-80% resolve in 6 months); mucosal bleeding → corticosteroids.
