questions.stem: A 5-year-old presents with petechiae and platelets of 20 × 10⁹/L. Which additional finding is the strongest indication for a bone marrow examination?
options: Large platelets on the blood film
Neutrophils of 0.6 × 10⁹/L and bone pain
A viral illness 3 weeks earlier
Wet purpura in the mouth
questions.explain: Another cell line low, hepatosplenomegaly or bone pain suggests leukaemia or aplasia and requires marrow examination. Large platelets and a preceding virus support ITP; mucosal bleeding changes treatment, not the diagnosis.
questions.note: Other cell line low, HSM or bone pain → bone marrow; TTP: raised LDH.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old has lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding. Platelet count and size are normal, but platelets fail to aggregate with ADP, collagen and adrenaline while ristocetin agglutination is normal. What is the diagnosis?
options: Bernard-Soulier syndrome
Von Willebrand disease
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
Glanzmann thrombasthenia
questions.explain: Glanzmann (GPIIb/IIIa deficiency) is an aggregation defect with normal count and normal ristocetin response. Bernard-Soulier (GPIb deficiency) is an adhesion defect with giant platelets, low count and absent ristocetin agglutination; vWD also gives abnormal ristocetin response.
questions.note: TTP: ADAMTS13 deficiency → uncleaved vWF → microthrombi; Glanzmann: aggregation defect; Bernard-Soulier: adhesion.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old has had ITP for 14 months with platelets persistently 15-25 × 10⁹/L and recurrent epistaxis despite courses of steroids and IVIG. What is the most appropriate next therapy?
options: A thrombopoietin receptor agonist such as eltrombopag or romiplostim
Elective splenectomy
Long-term daily prednisolone
Regular prophylactic platelet transfusions to keep platelets above 50
questions.explain: Chronic ITP (>12 months) with troublesome bleeding is treated with TPO receptor agonists (romiplostim/eltrombopag). Splenectomy is now deferred due to infection risk, and long-term steroids are avoided due to toxicity.
questions.note: Significant bleeding → IVIG; chronic ITP (>12 months): romiplostim/eltrombopag.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old recovering from pneumonia has a platelet count of 850 × 10⁹/L. What is the appropriate management?
options: Low-dose aspirin to prevent thrombosis
Bone marrow aspirate to exclude essential thrombocythaemia
No treatment; reactive thrombocytosis resolves with the underlying illness
Hydroxycarbamide until the count normalises
questions.explain: Thrombocytosis in children is almost always reactive (infection, inflammation, iron deficiency) and needs no treatment or aspirin; it does not carry thrombotic risk.
questions.note: TTP: plasma exchange; thrombocytosis is reactive → no treatment, no aspirin.

cards.front: Classify causes of thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction.
cards.back: Destruction: ITP, NAIT, TTP/HUS, DIC, hypersplenism • underproduction: leukaemia, aplasia • dysfunction with normal count: Glanzmann (aggregation), Bernard-Soulier (adhesion), vWD, aspirin.

cards.front: Stepwise management of childhood ITP.
cards.back: Cutaneous only → observe (75-80% resolve in 6 months) • mucosal bleeding → corticosteroids • significant bleeding → IVIG • chronic >12 months → romiplostim/eltrombopag.

cards.front: When does suspected ITP need a bone marrow?
cards.back: Another cell line low • hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy • bone pain • unwell child or atypical film • (no steroids before excluding leukaemia).

II-49.summary: DIC, HUS and TTP all consume platelets and fragment red cells; the clotting screen splits them: prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen and high D-dimer mean DIC, while HUS and TTP have normal clotting. Typical HUS follows bloody diarrhoea from STEC and is supportive only; atypical HUS gets eculizumab; TTP gets plasma exchange.

questions.stem: Which triad defines haemolytic uraemic syndrome?
options: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and hypertension
Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, fever and neurological signs
Iron-deficiency anaemia, thrombocytosis and haematuria
Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
questions.explain: HUS is MAHA plus thrombocytopenia plus AKI. Fever and neurological signs added to MAHA and thrombocytopenia make up the classic TTP pentad.
questions.note: DIC: consumptive coagulation. HUS triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old who had bloody diarrhoea after a farm visit 6 days ago now looks pale and has had little urine for 24 hours. Blood tests show Hb 68 g/L with schistocytes, platelets 40 × 10⁹/L and creatinine 280 µmol/L. Which organism is most likely responsible?
options: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC)
Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7
Salmonella enteritidis
Rotavirus
questions.explain: Typical HUS follows bloody diarrhoea from STEC (O157:H7), often from farm animals or undercooked beef. Shigella dysenteriae can also produce Shiga toxin, but the classic answer is STEC.
questions.note: Typical HUS follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (O157:H7).

questions.stem: What is the main mechanism of renal injury in typical HUS?
options: Immune complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane and activate complement
Bacteria directly invade renal tubules causing pyelonephritis
Shiga toxin binds Gb3 receptors on glomerular endothelium, causing microthrombi and RBC fragmentation
Hypovolaemia from diarrhoea causes acute tubular necrosis only
questions.explain: Shiga toxin binds Gb3 on glomerular endothelial cells, damaging them and producing platelet-fibrin microthrombi that fragment red cells and obstruct glomeruli. Immune-complex disease describes post-infectious GN.
questions.note: Shiga toxin binds Gb3 receptors on glomerular endothelium → microthrombi → RBC fragmentation, AKI.

questions.stem: In the child with typical STEC-HUS described above, which management is most appropriate?
options: Supportive care: fluids, electrolytes, transfusion and dialysis if needed
Intravenous ciprofloxacin to eradicate the organism and stop further toxin production
Loperamide to reduce ongoing diarrhoeal losses
Eculizumab infusion as first-line therapy
questions.explain: Typical HUS is managed supportively, with dialysis for AKI. Antibiotics and antimotility drugs are avoided because they may increase toxin release/absorption and HUS risk. Eculizumab is for atypical (complement-mediated) HUS.
questions.note: Typical HUS: supportive care, dialysis; avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs.

questions.stem: A child in septic shock is oozing from cannula sites and has purpura. Which set of results confirms disseminated intravascular coagulation?
options: Low platelets, prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen and high D-dimer
Low platelets, normal PT and APTT, normal fibrinogen and raised LDH
Normal platelets, prolonged APTT only, normal fibrinogen and normal D-dimer
High platelets, short PT and APTT, high fibrinogen and normal D-dimer
questions.explain: DIC consumes platelets and clotting factors (prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen) with fibrinolysis (high D-dimer). Normal clotting with low platelets and high LDH suggests HUS/TTP; isolated prolonged APTT suggests haemophilia or vWD.
questions.note: DIC labs: low platelets, prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer.

questions.stem: Two children have schistocytes, thrombocytopenia and AKI. Child A has a prolonged PT and APTT; Child B has normal clotting times. What is the most useful interpretation?
options: Child A favours HUS; Child B favours DIC
Both favour DIC, as clotting times vary with disease stage
Child A favours DIC; Child B favours HUS or TTP
Child A favours TTP; Child B favours DIC
questions.explain: Clotting times are normal in HUS and TTP (platelet-driven microthrombi) but prolonged in DIC (factor consumption). TTP additionally has markedly raised LDH and low ADAMTS13.
questions.note: Clotting times are normal in HUS but prolonged in DIC; TTP has raised LDH.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old develops MAHA, thrombocytopenia and AKI without any preceding diarrhoea; her uncle had a similar illness. Stool STEC testing is negative and C3 is low. What is the most likely mechanism and treatment?
options: ADAMTS13 deficiency; plasma exchange
Dysregulated alternative complement pathway; eculizumab
Shiga toxin-mediated endothelial injury; supportive care
Factor consumption from sepsis; FFP and cryoprecipitate
questions.explain: Atypical HUS is due to alternative complement pathway dysregulation (often familial, low C3) and responds to the C5 inhibitor eculizumab. ADAMTS13 deficiency is TTP, treated with plasma exchange.
questions.note: Atypical HUS: alternative complement pathway dysregulation.

questions.stem: A child with meningococcal sepsis has DIC with platelets 30 × 10⁹/L and fibrinogen 0.8 g/L but no bleeding. What is the most important management principle?
options: Transfuse platelets, FFP and cryoprecipitate to normalise the numbers
Start a heparin infusion to stop microthrombus formation
Give tranexamic acid to inhibit fibrinolysis
Treat the underlying sepsis; give blood products only if bleeding or before procedures
questions.explain: DIC is treated by treating the cause; platelets, FFP and cryoprecipitate are given only for bleeding (or high-risk procedures). Routine heparin or antifibrinolytics are not recommended.
questions.note: DIC: treat the cause; platelets, FFP, cryo only if bleeding.

cards.front: How do you distinguish DIC, HUS and TTP in the lab?
cards.back: DIC: low platelets, prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer • HUS: MAHA, low platelets, AKI, normal clotting • TTP: normal clotting, very raised LDH, low ADAMTS13.

cards.front: Classify HUS and give the treatment of each.
cards.back: Typical: STEC O157:H7 after bloody diarrhoea → supportive, dialysis, no antibiotics/antimotility • atypical: alternative complement dysregulation → eculizumab • (TTP: ADAMTS13 → plasma exchange, steroids, rituximab).

cards.front: Causes and management of DIC.
cards.back: Sepsis, shock, trauma, malignancy • tissue factor → microthrombi + consumption + fibrinolysis • treat the cause; platelets, FFP, cryo only if bleeding.

II-50.summary: Porphyrias are haem-synthesis blocks: early precursors (ALA, PBG) are neurotoxic and give acute attacks (AIP: abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric change, dark urine, no photosensitivity), while late porphyrins give photosensitivity (PCT, EPP). Screen an attack with urinary PBG and treat with haem arginate and glucose; avoid P450 inducers.

questions.stem: Which enzyme is deficient in acute intermittent porphyria, and how is it inherited?
options: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase; autosomal dominant
Ferrochelatase; autosomal recessive
Porphobilinogen deaminase (HMBS); autosomal dominant
ALA dehydratase; autosomal recessive
questions.explain: AIP is an autosomal dominant deficiency of PBG deaminase (HMBS). UROD deficiency causes PCT; ferrochelatase deficiency causes EPP.
questions.note: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP): autosomal dominant, deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (HMBS).

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl has severe colicky abdominal pain with a soft abdomen, vomiting, tachycardia, anxiety and hallucinations, and proximal limb weakness 3 days after starting carbamazepine. Her urine darkens on standing. Her skin is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute intermittent porphyria
Porphyria cutanea tarda
Erythropoietic protoporphyria
Lead poisoning
questions.explain: Wine-coloured urine, an inducer, psychological disturbance, abdominal pain and neuropathy without photosensitivity is AIP (Wine In PAIN). PCT and EPP are cutaneous porphyrias; lead poisoning causes anaemia with basophilic stippling.
questions.note: AIP mnemonic Wine In PAIN: wine-coloured urine, inducers, psychological disturbance, abdominal pain, neuropathy; no photosensitivity.

questions.stem: In the girl above, which is the best initial screening test during the attack?
options: Faecal protoporphyrin
Plasma ferritin
Erythrocyte free protoporphyrin
Urinary porphobilinogen
questions.explain: During an acute attack urinary PBG (and ALA) is markedly raised; this is the key screening test. Erythrocyte protoporphyrin is raised in EPP, faecal porphyrins help with variegate/hereditary coproporphyria.
questions.note: Screening test in an acute attack: urinary porphobilinogen; also raised ALA.

questions.stem: During the acute porphyric attack, her sodium falls to 121 mmol/L with concentrated urine and euvolaemia. What is the most likely cause?
options: Primary adrenal insufficiency with mineralocorticoid deficiency
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
Cerebral salt wasting
Gastrointestinal losses from vomiting
questions.explain: Hyponatraemia in an acute porphyric attack is due to SIADH (hypothalamic involvement): euvolaemic with concentrated urine. Vomiting losses cause hypovolaemia; cerebral salt wasting is hypovolaemic.
questions.note: Hyponatraemia in an attack is due to SIADH.

questions.stem: What is the specific treatment of a severe acute attack of AIP?
options: Intravenous phenobarbital and fluids
Intravenous haem arginate (haemin) and glucose
Oral hydroxychloroquine and phlebotomy
Beta-carotene and sun avoidance
questions.explain: Haem and glucose suppress ALA synthase, reducing production of neurotoxic precursors. Barbiturates are contraindicated as they induce ALA synthase; hydroxychloroquine/phlebotomy treat PCT; beta-carotene is for EPP.
questions.note: Acute attack: IV haem arginate (haemin) and glucose, which inhibit ALA synthesis.

questions.stem: Why do patients with AIP have neurovisceral attacks but no photosensitivity, unlike PCT?
options: The block is late, so photoactive porphyrins accumulate only in the liver
ALA and PBG are photoactive but are excreted too fast to reach the skin
Haem excess in AIP protects the skin from ultraviolet damage
The block is early, so neurotoxic ALA and PBG accumulate, not photoactive porphyrins
questions.explain: Precursors before the block accumulate: in AIP these are ALA and PBG (neurotoxic, not photosensitising). In PCT and EPP the block is later, so porphyrins accumulate and react with light.
questions.note: Early haem precursors (ALA, PBG) are neurotoxic → acute attacks.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old cries and scratches within minutes of sun exposure, with burning pain, redness and swelling of the hands but no blisters. Which porphyria is most likely, and which enzyme is deficient?
options: Erythropoietic protoporphyria; ferrochelatase
Porphyria cutanea tarda; uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
Acute intermittent porphyria; porphobilinogen deaminase
Congenital erythropoietic porphyria; ALA synthase
questions.explain: EPP is the commonest porphyria in children: immediate painful non-blistering photosensitivity due to ferrochelatase deficiency. PCT (UROD) is the commonest overall but gives delayed blistering in adults; AIP has no photosensitivity.
questions.note: Commonest in children: erythropoietic protoporphyria, ferrochelatase deficiency. Triggers: P-450 inducers, barbiturates contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old with fragile skin, blisters on the backs of the hands and hyperpigmentation is diagnosed with porphyria cutanea tarda. Which treatment is appropriate?
options: Intravenous haem arginate and glucose
High-dose hydroxychloroquine daily
Low-dose hydroxychloroquine or regular phlebotomy
Oral iron supplementation with vitamin C to aid absorption
questions.explain: PCT (UROD deficiency) responds to phlebotomy (iron depletion) or low-dose hydroxychloroquine; high doses can cause hepatotoxicity. Iron worsens PCT; haem is for acute porphyrias.
questions.note: PCT: low-dose hydroxychloroquine or phlebotomy.

cards.front: Compare acute and cutaneous porphyrias.
cards.back: Acute (AIP, PBG deaminase, AD): early precursors ALA/PBG → neurovisceral attacks, no photosensitivity • cutaneous: PCT (UROD, commonest overall), EPP (ferrochelatase, commonest in children) → porphyrins → photosensitivity.

cards.front: What are the features of an acute AIP attack (Wine In PAIN)?
cards.back: Wine-coloured urine • Inducers (P450 inducers, barbiturates) • Psychological disturbance • Abdominal pain • Neuropathy • plus hyponatraemia (SIADH) • screen: urinary PBG.

cards.front: Management of porphyrias.
cards.back: Acute attack: IV haem arginate + glucose (inhibit ALA synthase), avoid P450 inducers/barbiturates • PCT: low-dose hydroxychloroquine or phlebotomy • EPP: sun protection.
